Face Similarity Analysis

Deep Learning for Objective Lineup Fairness Assessment

Colin G. Tredoux

Tamsyn M. Naylor

2026-10-30

Source: vignettes/face_similarity.Rmd
face_similarity.Rmd

Acknowledgement. Large language models supplied by Anthropic and OpenAI were used in preparing this vignette, to assist with checking code, testing the veracity of the approaches described, and on occasion editing the text. Responsibility for the content rests with the authors.

Note on the code in this vignette. Unlike the other vignettes in this package, the examples below are not executed when it is built. They require two things the package cannot supply: a working Python environment with DeepFace installed, and face image files of your own. No face images are distributed with r4lineups, for obvious reasons. The code is exactly what would run against your own images, but the outputs shown in the prose are described rather than computed.

Introduction

r4lineups provides deep learning methods for measuring facial similarity in eyewitness lineups. These tools complement mock-witness studies by giving analysts reproducible, continuous similarity summaries that can help screen candidate foils and document visual fairness checks. They should be treated as exploratory aids, not as a replacement for mock-witness or outcome-based evidence.

Why measure face similarity?

Traditional lineup fairness assessment relies on mock witnesses viewing the lineup and choosing from it on the basis of a description. That dependence is the method’s foundation, and it is also where its difficulties lie.

Whose description? The mock-witness procedure asks people to pick the member who best matches a description, so the result is a property of the description-lineup pair, not of the lineup alone. Change the description and the measured fairness changes. In real cases the description is the witness’s own, given under conditions that may have been poor, and it is often the only one available. In laboratory studies it is frequently fabricated by the experimenters, which raises a different problem: a description written with a great deal of detail makes a lineup very hard to construct, because few candidate foils will match on every feature. Detail also tends to narrow the field towards the suspect, so an over-specified description can make a perfectly reasonable lineup look unfair — and an under-specified one can make an unfair lineup look acceptable.

Beyond that, the procedure requires recruiting and testing participants, which is slow and costly, and returns categorical data — which member each mock witness chose — rather than a continuous measure of resemblance.

Deep learning face similarity measures something different: the resemblance between the images themselves, with no description and no participants. It is numeric, fast, scalable to hundreds of lineups, and exactly reproducible — the same images always give the same scores. It can also say which foils sit close to or far from the suspect, which a choice distribution can only do indirectly.

An important caution before going further

It is tempting to move from “we can measure similarity” to “here is the right amount of similarity”, and this vignette deliberately does not do that.

The literature is not settled on how similar lineup foils should be. The long-standing intuition that foils should closely resemble the suspect competes with evidence that very high similarity can impair discriminability by removing the diagnostic features a witness might use, and the balance appears to depend on the procedure, the encoding conditions and what is being optimised. There is no agreed optimum, and no threshold at which a lineup becomes “fair” on a similarity metric.

So the functions here report degree of similarity; they do not grade it. Where the sections below give numbers, read them as descriptions of the images, not as verdicts on the lineup. Similarity scores are most defensible used comparatively — this foil against that one, this lineup against another constructed the same way — and as a screening aid during construction, rather than as evidence of fairness after the fact. The choice-based measures in the main vignette, and the outcome-based measures elsewhere in the package, remain the evidence about how a lineup actually performed.

  1. Setup - Installing Python dependencies
  2. Basic Comparison - Comparing two face images
  3. Lineup Analysis - Analyzing entire lineups
  4. Models & Metrics - Choosing the right configuration
  5. Visualization - Displaying results

Setup

Face similarity analysis uses Python’s DeepFace library via R’s reticulate package. This requires a one-time setup.

Check Current Setup 

library(r4lineups)

# Check if Python and dependencies are available
check_python_deps()

Install Python Dependencies

If you don’t have the required dependencies, install them:

The setup has one requirement that catches most people out, so it is worth doing in the right order.

TensorFlow, which DeepFace depends on, does not publish wheels for every Python version. At the time of writing it supports Python 3.9 to 3.12. If your system Python is newer — 3.13 or 3.14, which is increasingly common — the install will proceed a long way and then fail with No matching distribution found for tensorflow. install_r4lineups_python() checks the interpreter first and stops before downloading anything, rather than letting that happen.

So pin the version, and obtain a suitable interpreter before asking for an environment built from one:

# Step 1: get a Python that TensorFlow supports. Skip if you already have one.
reticulate::install_python(version = "3.11")

# Step 2: build the environment from it and install DeepFace
install_r4lineups_python(envname = "r4lineups-face-env",
                         python_version = "3.11")

Requesting python_version = "3.11" without step 1 fails, because there is no 3.11 interpreter to build from. Earlier versions of this package passed that straight through to reticulate, which reported

Suitable Python installation for creating a venv not found.
Requested version constraint: 3.11

without saying how to obtain one. The package now checks first and reports which versions it did find, along with the reticulate::install_python() call needed.

The first run takes several minutes, as it downloads the deep learning models (ArcFace, FaceNet and others). They are cached afterwards.

If the Python setup defeats you

It is a genuine possibility — the dependency chain is long and platform dependent. Two fallbacks:

  • The bundled Shiny application, run_r4lineups_app(), covers the lineup fairness measures that need no Python at all.
  • Everything in the rest of this package — effective size, functional size, ROC, CAC, the SDT and MPT models — is pure R. Face similarity is the only component with a Python dependency, and it is an optional adjunct rather than a prerequisite for anything else.

Verify Installation 

# Check available models
available_models()

# Check available face detectors
available_detectors()

Basic Face Comparison

The simplest use case is comparing two face images.

Compare Two Faces 

# Compare target to a foil
# (Use your own image paths)
result <- face_similarity(
  img1_path = "path/to/target.jpg",
  img2_path = "path/to/foil1.jpg",
  model = "ArcFace",     # State-of-the-art face recognition model
  metric = "cosine"      # Similarity metric
)

print(result)

Understanding the Output 

# Similarity score (0-1, higher = more similar)
result$similarity  # e.g., 0.85 = very similar

# Distance (lower = more similar)
result$distance    # e.g., 0.15

# Would the model judge these to be the same person?
result$verified    # see the note below on what this does and does not mean

# Model's threshold for verification
result$threshold   # e.g., 0.68 for ArcFace + cosine

Reading the output. similarity is a continuous score on the model’s own scale; higher means the two images are closer in the model’s embedding space. There is deliberately no table of bands here, because — as set out above — the literature does not establish what level of similarity a lineup foil ought to have. Compare scores against each other, not against a standard.

verified is different, and it is worth separating clearly. It is not a judgement about fairness; it is the model’s identity decision — whether the two images are of the same person. A TRUE here does carry a definite implication, but a narrow one: if the model cannot distinguish the foil from the suspect, the foil is arguably not functioning as an alternative at all, and the lineup may effectively contain the suspect twice. That is a construction error, detectable without any claim about optimal similarity.

threshold is the model’s own cut-off for that identity decision, and it varies by model and metric — it is not a fairness criterion.

Lineup Similarity Analysis

Analyze all lineup members against the target in one call.

Analyze Complete Lineup 

# Analyze all foils in a lineup
lineup_result <- lineup_similarity(
  target_path = "path/to/target.jpg",
  foil_paths = c(
    "path/to/foil1.jpg",
    "path/to/foil2.jpg",
    "path/to/foil3.jpg",
    "path/to/foil4.jpg",
    "path/to/foil5.jpg"
  ),
  model = "ArcFace",
  metric = "cosine"
)

print(lineup_result)

Examining Results 

# View as dataframe
lineup_result

# Summary statistics
summary(lineup_result)

# Foils the model judges to be the same identity as the suspect. These are
# worth inspecting by eye: a foil indistinguishable from the suspect is not
# functioning as an alternative.
same_identity <- lineup_result[lineup_result$verified, ]
if (nrow(same_identity) > 0) {
  cat("Model judges these foils to be the same person as the target:\n")
  print(same_identity[, c("foil_path", "similarity")])
}

# Check similarity distribution
cat("Mean similarity:", round(mean(lineup_result$similarity), 3), "\n")
cat("SD similarity:", round(sd(lineup_result$similarity), 3), "\n")
cat("Range:", range(lineup_result$similarity), "\n")

Describing the similarity profile

The heading here is deliberately not “fairness assessment”. What these numbers describe is the similarity profile of the lineup — where the foils sit relative to the suspect and to each other. Turning that into a verdict would require knowing what profile is desirable, which is exactly what is unsettled.

Three quantities are worth reporting:

  • Mean similarity — how close the foils are to the suspect on average.
  • Spread of similarity — whether the foils are homogeneous, or whether one or two sit much closer to the suspect than the rest. This is often the more informative of the two, since a lineup where one foil resembles the suspect far more than the others is unbalanced whatever the mean.
  • Identity matches — foils the model cannot distinguish from the suspect, as discussed above.
# Describe the similarity profile
mean_sim <- mean(lineup_result$similarity)
sd_sim <- sd(lineup_result$similarity)
n_verified <- sum(lineup_result$verified)

cat("Similarity profile:\n")
cat("  Mean similarity:", round(mean_sim, 3), "\n")
cat("  SD of similarity:", round(sd_sim, 3), "\n")
cat("  Range:", round(range(lineup_result$similarity), 3), "\n")
cat("  Foils judged same identity:", n_verified, "\n\n")

# The one flag worth raising automatically, because it is an identity decision
# rather than a fairness judgement
if (n_verified > 0) {
  cat("Note:", n_verified, "foil(s) judged the same person as the target.\n")
  cat("Inspect these by eye; they may not be functioning as alternatives.\n")
}

Models and Metrics

Different models and metrics serve different purposes.

Available Models 

# List all models
available_models()

# Models in order of recommendation for lineup research:
# 1. ArcFace    - State-of-the-art, best overall performance
# 2. Facenet512 - Very good, slightly faster than ArcFace
# 3. Facenet    - Good, faster inference
# 4. VGG-Face   - Older but reliable baseline
# 5. OpenFace   - Fastest, lower accuracy

Distance Metrics 

# Three metrics available:

# 1. Cosine (RECOMMENDED for most cases)
#    - Range: [0, 1] (can convert to similarity)
#    - Focuses on angle between embeddings
#    - Most commonly used in face recognition

# 2. Euclidean L2 (normalized Euclidean)
#    - Normalized vector distance
#    - Good for comparing across models

# 3. Euclidean
#    - Raw vector distance
#    - Less commonly used

Comparing Models 

# Compare different models on same lineup
models_to_test <- c("ArcFace", "Facenet512", "VGG-Face")

comparison_results <- list()

for (model in models_to_test) {
  result <- lineup_similarity(
    target_path = "path/to/target.jpg",
    foil_paths = foil_paths,
    model = model,
    metric = "cosine"
  )

  comparison_results[[model]] <- data.frame(
    model = model,
    mean_similarity = mean(result$similarity),
    sd_similarity = sd(result$similarity),
    n_verified = sum(result$verified)
  )
}

comparison_df <- do.call(rbind, comparison_results)
print(comparison_df)

Interpretation: - Models may give different absolute scores - But relative ordering (which foils are most similar) usually consistent - Use same model consistently within a study - ArcFace generally most accurate

Visualization

Display Lineup with Similarity Scores 

# Create visual display of lineup
display_lineup(
  target_path = "path/to/target.jpg",
  foil_paths = foil_paths,
  similarity_scores = lineup_result$similarity,
  labels = paste("Foil", 1:5),
  title = "Lineup Similarity Analysis"
)

# Save the visualization
ggsave("lineup_display.png", width = 10, height = 8)

Similarity Heatmap 

# For multiple lineups, create heatmap
library(ggplot2)

# Suppose we have analyzed multiple lineups
lineup_ids <- c("Lineup_1", "Lineup_2", "Lineup_3")
foil_positions <- 1:5

# Create example data (replace with your actual data)
similarity_matrix <- matrix(
  runif(15, 0.3, 0.8),  # Example data
  nrow = 3,
  ncol = 5,
  dimnames = list(lineup_ids, paste("Foil", foil_positions))
)

# Convert to long format for ggplot
library(reshape2)
sim_long <- melt(similarity_matrix)
colnames(sim_long) <- c("Lineup", "Foil", "Similarity")

# Create heatmap
ggplot(sim_long, aes(x = Foil, y = Lineup, fill = Similarity)) +
  geom_tile(color = "white") +
  scale_fill_gradient2(
    low = "blue", mid = "yellow", high = "red",
    midpoint = 0.6,
    limits = c(0, 1)
  ) +
  geom_text(aes(label = round(Similarity, 2)), color = "black", size = 3) +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(title = "Lineup Similarity Heatmap",
       subtitle = "Color indicates target-foil similarity")

Similarity Distribution 

# Plot distribution of similarities
ggplot(lineup_result, aes(x = similarity)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 0.05, fill = "steelblue", color = "black") +
  geom_vline(aes(xintercept = threshold),
             color = "red", linetype = "dashed", size = 1) +
  annotate("text", x = threshold, y = Inf,
           label = "Verification\nThreshold",
           vjust = 1.5, color = "red") +
  labs(
    title = "Distribution of Target-Foil Similarity",
    x = "Similarity Score",
    y = "Count"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()

Advanced Features

Extract Face Embeddings

Embeddings are the deep learning representations of faces. They can be used for advanced analyses.

# Get embedding for a face
embedding <- get_embedding(
  img_path = "path/to/face.jpg",
  model = "ArcFace"
)

# Embedding is a numeric vector (typically 512 dimensions)
length(embedding)  # 512 for ArcFace

# Get embeddings for comparison
result_with_emb <- face_similarity(
  img1_path = "path/to/target.jpg",
  img2_path = "path/to/foil.jpg",
  model = "ArcFace",
  return_embeddings = TRUE
)

target_embedding <- result_with_emb$embeddings$img1
foil_embedding <- result_with_emb$embeddings$img2

Dimensionality Reduction Visualization

Visualize lineup in 2D space using embeddings:

# Requires Rtsne package
library(Rtsne)

# Collect embeddings for all lineup members
all_embeddings <- list()

# Target embedding
all_embeddings[["Target"]] <- get_embedding("path/to/target.jpg", model = "ArcFace")

# Foil embeddings
for (i in seq_along(foil_paths)) {
  all_embeddings[[paste0("Foil_", i)]] <- get_embedding(foil_paths[i], model = "ArcFace")
}

# Convert to matrix
embedding_matrix <- do.call(rbind, all_embeddings)

# Run t-SNE
set.seed(42)
tsne_result <- Rtsne(embedding_matrix, dims = 2, perplexity = 2)

# Create visualization dataframe
viz_df <- data.frame(
  x = tsne_result$Y[, 1],
  y = tsne_result$Y[, 2],
  member = names(all_embeddings),
  type = ifelse(names(all_embeddings) == "Target", "Target", "Foil")
)

# Plot
ggplot(viz_df, aes(x = x, y = y, color = type, label = member)) +
  geom_point(size = 4) +
  geom_text(vjust = -1) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("Target" = "red", "Foil" = "blue")) +
  labs(
    title = "Lineup Members in Embedding Space",
    subtitle = "t-SNE projection of face embeddings",
    x = "t-SNE Dimension 1",
    y = "t-SNE Dimension 2"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")

Batch Processing Multiple Lineups 

# Process multiple lineups efficiently
lineup_list <- list(
  lineup1 = list(target = "target1.jpg", foils = c("1a.jpg", "1b.jpg", "1c.jpg")),
  lineup2 = list(target = "target2.jpg", foils = c("2a.jpg", "2b.jpg", "2c.jpg")),
  lineup3 = list(target = "target3.jpg", foils = c("3a.jpg", "3b.jpg", "3c.jpg"))
)

# Analyze all lineups
results_list <- lapply(names(lineup_list), function(lineup_name) {
  lineup <- lineup_list[[lineup_name]]

  result <- lineup_similarity(
    target_path = lineup$target,
    foil_paths = lineup$foils,
    model = "ArcFace"
  )

  # Add lineup identifier
  result$lineup_id <- lineup_name

  result
})

# Combine results
all_results <- do.call(rbind, results_list)

# Summary by lineup
library(dplyr)
lineup_summary <- all_results %>%
  group_by(lineup_id) %>%
  summarise(
    mean_similarity = mean(similarity),
    sd_similarity = sd(similarity),
    min_similarity = min(similarity),
    max_similarity = max(similarity),
    n_verified = sum(verified)
  )

print(lineup_summary)

Integration with Traditional Measures

Combine deep learning similarity with traditional lineup fairness measures.

Compare with Effective Size 

# Traditional effective size from mock witnesses
# (Using example data)
mock_choices <- c(3, 2, 5, 6, 1, 3, 3, 5, 6, 4)  # Position 3 is suspect
trad_eff_size <- esize_T(table(factor(mock_choices, levels = 1:6)))

cat("Traditional effective size:", round(trad_eff_size, 2), "\n")

# Face similarity, for comparison. Note these measure different things:
# effective size describes how mock witnesses distributed their choices,
# similarity describes the images themselves.
mean_similarity <- mean(lineup_result$similarity)

cat("Mean face similarity:", round(mean_similarity, 3), "\n")

# Correlation across multiple lineups
# (With sufficient data, examine relationship)

Similarity-Weighted Effective Size

Create a hybrid measure:

The direction of the relationship matters here, and it is easy to state backwards. Mock witnesses choose the member who best matches the description. A foil that closely resembles the suspect also resembles the description, so it draws choices away from the suspect — which is precisely what makes a lineup fair. A foil that resembles the suspect very little matches the description poorly and tends to be chosen by nobody: it is a null foil, and it contributes nothing.

So the expectation runs: higher foil-suspect similarity should mean a higher share of mock-witness choices, and hence a larger effective size.

# Expected selection shares implied by similarity. Foils more similar to the
# suspect match the description better and should attract more choices.
similarities <- lineup_result$similarity
expected_prob <- similarities / sum(similarities)

# Compare to observed selections
# observed_prob <- table(mock_choices[-which(mock_choices == suspect_pos)]) /
#                  length(mock_choices[-which(mock_choices == suspect_pos)])

# Similarity-adjusted bias metric
# (Larger discrepancy = more bias after accounting for appearance)

Validation Studies

Examine predictive validity:

# Research question: Do objective similarity scores predict mock witness choices?

# For each lineup:
# - Get face similarity scores
# - Collect mock witness data
# - Correlate: Do more similar foils get chosen more often?

# Example correlation structure (use your data):
# cor.test(foil_similarities, foil_selection_rates)

Practical Guidelines

Interpreting Similarity Scores

Similarity ranges (for ArcFace + cosine): - > 0.80: Very high similarity - likely lineup bias - 0.70-0.80: High similarity - check if acceptable for your context - 0.55-0.70: Moderate similarity - generally acceptable - 0.40-0.55: Low similarity - foils sufficiently different - < 0.40: Very low similarity - foils may not match description

Context matters: - Acceptable similarity depends on description specificity - More specific descriptions allow tighter similarity ranges - Less specific descriptions require broader ranges

Best Practices

  1. Consistency
    • Use same model throughout a study
    • Use same metric throughout a study
    • Use same verification thresholds
  2. Validation
    • Compare similarity scores to mock witness data when available
    • Validate that your similarity threshold makes sense for your context
  3. Complementarity
    • Use face similarity alongside traditional mock witness studies
    • Objective similarity + subjective judgments provide comprehensive assessment
  4. Documentation
    • Report model and metric used
    • Report mean and SD of similarities
    • Report verification threshold and number verified
  5. Image Quality
    • Use high-quality, front-facing photos
    • Ensure good lighting and resolution
    • Consistent photo conditions across lineup members

Troubleshooting

“No face detected” - Image quality too poor - Face not front-facing enough - Try different detector: detector = "opencv" is more lenient

Embeddings fail - Check image file paths are correct - Ensure images are standard formats (jpg, png) - Verify Python environment is activated

Inconsistent results - Deep learning models are deterministic - If results change, check if images were modified - Verify same model/metric used

Very high/low similarities - Check image quality - Verify correct target-foil pairing - Consider if lineup truly is biased/fair

Example Workflow

Complete analysis from start to finish:

# 1. Setup (first time only)
# install_r4lineups_python()

# 2. Load package
library(r4lineups)

# 3. Analyze lineup
lineup_sim <- lineup_similarity(
  target_path = "suspect_photo.jpg",
  foil_paths = c("foil1.jpg", "foil2.jpg", "foil3.jpg",
                 "foil4.jpg", "foil5.jpg"),
  model = "ArcFace",
  metric = "cosine"
)

# 4. Assess fairness
mean_sim <- mean(lineup_sim$similarity)
sd_sim <- sd(lineup_sim$similarity)
n_verified <- sum(lineup_sim$verified)

# 5. Generate report
cat("=== Lineup Fairness Report ===\n\n")
cat("Objective Similarity Analysis\n")
cat("Model: ArcFace | Metric: Cosine\n\n")
cat("Results:\n")
cat("  Mean similarity:", round(mean_sim, 3), "\n")
cat("  SD similarity:", round(sd_sim, 3), "\n")
cat("  Range:", round(min(lineup_sim$similarity), 3), "-",
    round(max(lineup_sim$similarity), 3), "\n")
cat("  Verified as same person:", n_verified, "of 5 foils\n\n")

if (mean_sim > 0.7 || n_verified > 0) {
  cat("CONCERN: High similarity indicates potential lineup bias\n")
} else if (mean_sim < 0.55) {
  cat("ACCEPTABLE: Foils sufficiently dissimilar from target\n")
} else {
  cat("BORDERLINE: Consider additional assessment\n")
}

# 6. Visualize
display_lineup(
  target_path = "suspect_photo.jpg",
  foil_paths = c("foil1.jpg", "foil2.jpg", "foil3.jpg",
                 "foil4.jpg", "foil5.jpg"),
  similarity_scores = lineup_sim$similarity,
  title = "Lineup 001 - Similarity Analysis"
)

# 7. Save results
write.csv(lineup_sim, "lineup_001_similarity.csv", row.names = FALSE)

  • Schroff, F., Kalenichenko, D., & Philbin, J. (2015). FaceNet: A unified embedding for face recognition and clustering. CVPR 2015.

Technical Details

What is computed

Each image is passed through a pretrained deep face-recognition network, which maps it to an embedding — a vector, typically 128 or 512 dimensional, positioned so that images of the same person land close together. Similarity between two faces is then a distance in that space, converted to a similarity score.

Component Meaning
model Which network produces the embedding (ArcFace, FaceNet, VGG-Face, …). Different networks give different embedding spaces, so scores are not comparable across models
metric How distance is measured in that space — cosine, Euclidean, or Euclidean on L2-normalised vectors
similarity Distance converted to a 0-1 scale, higher meaning closer
threshold The model’s own cut-off for judging two images the same identity. Model- and metric-specific
verified Whether the distance falls inside that threshold

Assumptions and limitations

  1. Scores are model-relative. ArcFace and FaceNet place faces in different spaces. Never compare a similarity score from one against another, and always report which model and metric produced a number.
  2. The networks were trained for recognition, not for lineup construction. They are optimised to tell identities apart, which is related to but not the same as capturing what makes two faces look alike to a witness. Whether the embedding distance corresponds to human perceived similarity is an empirical question, and the appropriate reference here is Tredoux (2002) on direct similarity measurement and its relation to human judgements.
  3. Image conditions matter. Pose, lighting, expression, resolution and background all affect embeddings. Lineup photographs taken under different conditions may differ in similarity for reasons that have nothing to do with facial resemblance. Standardised images are essential.
  4. Demographic differences in accuracy are well documented for face recognition systems, with error rates varying by ethnicity, sex and age. That is a serious caution in a forensic context, where the consequences of systematic error fall unevenly.
  5. No fairness threshold exists. The point of the caution at the top of this vignette, restated: these functions describe similarity, they do not adjudicate fairness.

Reproducibility

Given the same images, model and metric, scores are exactly reproducible — one of the method’s genuine advantages over mock-witness testing. Record the model, the metric and the package versions, since a different DeepFace release may ship different weights.
